paper.title: Thyroid Nodule Segmentation in Ultrasound Images with Conformal Uncertainty Estimation
paper.abstract: Thyroid nodules affect a large proportion of the general population. Although most are benign, a non-negligible fraction is malignant. Ultrasound imaging is the primary diagnostic modality, and accurate nodule segmentation is a prerequisite for CAD systems to classify malignancy and assess metastatic risk.\\ In this work, we propose a thyroid nodule segmentation framework that integrates a DeepLabV3+, channel-attention modules and post-hoc conformal prediction, providing both accurate mask and pixel-level uncertainty estimates. We address thyroid ultrasound nodule segmentation as the first stage of a pipeline that also includes malignancy classification and metastatic risk prediction. We adopt DeepLabV3+, whose Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) captures multi-scale context, with an EfficientNet-B5 backbone for its accuracy-efficiency trade-off. Additionally, we test three channel-attention modules: Squeeze-and-Excitation, CBAM and Grouped Channel Attention (GCA), paired with two loss formulations (Dice-BCE and Boundary).\\ Since binary masks do not indicate prediction confidence, we wrap the trained model with a split conformal prediction layer that produces pixel-level uncertainty maps with statistical coverage guarantees.\\ We evaluate all configurations on the TN3K public benchmark using a fixed split and directly compare them with state-of-the-art methods. The plain backbone already improves upon previously reported results, with CBAM + Dice-BCE emerging as the best overall configuration.

paper.title: Beamforming Design for RIS-Assisted Backscatter NOMA in Underlay Cognitive Radio
paper.abstract: This paper investigates a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted backscatter non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) network operating as the secondary system of an underlay cognitive radio network. A multi-antenna base station serves several user clusters through the RIS, each containing a backscatter device (BD). We maximise the weighted sum rate of the secondary network by jointly optimising the transmit beamformers and the RIS reflection matrix, subject to the power budget, the interference-temperature limit and minimum rate requirements. The non-convex problem is solved by alternating optimisation, using semidefinite relaxation and sequential rank-one constraint relaxation. Interference-normalised user ordering makes the successive interference cancellation constraints redundant. A closed-form equal-rate power split is derived; it agrees closely with simulation and costs about 4.5% of the sum rate. Supporting the BDs reduces the NOMA sum rate by 8.7% relative to a no-BD design, while a larger BD reflection coefficient raises the backscatter rate with little NOMA loss.

paper.title: MedImageOSWorld: Benchmarking GUI Agents for Medical Image Consoles
paper.abstract: Graphical consoles offer a practical interface for medical acquisition assistance, allowing agents to work through the controls and visual feedback used by human operators. Reliable assistance requires linking on-screen anatomy to acquisition decisions that determine what image evidence becomes available next. We introduce MedImageOSWorld, a benchmark for evaluating this capability in simulated CT, MR, and ultrasound consoles. Using screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions, agents configure protocols, plan acquisitions, inspect the resulting images, and make corrective adjustments across seven capability levels, from console operation to feedback-driven control. Evaluation combines task-specific workflow checks with hidden anatomical ground truth to assess procedural completion and acquisition outcomes separately. A common evaluation protocol specifies episode conditions and interaction budgets, while recorded trajectories support analysis of how agents observe, act, and respond to acquisition feedback. Across eleven open-weight agents, success rates range from 3.0 to 25.0 on a 0-100 scale while workflow-progress rates reach 21.5-74.5: agents complete much of the console workflow but rarely acquire the intended anatomy. Success collapses between perception and planning, from 79-90% at the lowest three levels for the best agent to at most 12% for millimetre-level planning and 0% for closed-loop control among open-weight agents. Two proprietary agents reach success rates of about 34 and exceed the best open-weight agent mainly in acquisition quality (61 versus 42). MedImageOSWorld provides a controlled setting for studying whether general-purpose GUI agents can translate visual observations into effective medical acquisition decisions.

\lhead{Preprint}
\begin{abstract}
  Graphical consoles offer a practical interface for medical acquisition
  assistance, allowing agents to work through the controls and visual feedback
  used by human operators. Reliable assistance requires linking on-screen
  anatomy to acquisition decisions that determine what image evidence becomes
  available next. We introduce MedImageOSWorld, a benchmark for evaluating this
  capability in simulated CT, MR, and ultrasound consoles. Using screenshots and mouse-and-keyboard actions, agents configure protocols, plan acquisitions, inspect the resulting images, and make corrective adjustments across seven capability levels, from console operation to feedback-driven control.
  Evaluation combines task-specific workflow checks with hidden anatomical
  ground truth to assess procedural completion and acquisition outcomes
  separately. A common evaluation protocol specifies episode conditions and
  interaction budgets, while recorded trajectories support analysis of how
  agents observe, act, and respond to acquisition feedback. Across eleven
  open-weight agents, success rates range from 3.0 to 25.0 on a 0--100 scale
  while workflow-progress rates reach 21.5--74.5: agents complete much of the
  console workflow but rarely acquire the intended anatomy. Success collapses
  between perception and planning, from 79--90\
  the best agent to at most 12\
  closed-loop control among open-weight agents. Two proprietary agents reach success rates of about 34
  and exceed the best open-weight agent mainly in acquisition quality (61
  versus 42). MedImageOSWorld provides a controlled setting for studying
  whether general-purpose GUI agents can translate visual observations into
  effective medical acquisition decisions. 
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}
Medical image acquisition depends on operators translating an examination
request into console actions. They configure protocols, plan anatomical
coverage or imaging planes, and assess the resulting images. The console is the interface where an operator turns an examination goal
into acquired image evidence. An inadequate
acquisition may require adjustment, repetition, or escalation. 
The graphical console is a natural interface for acquisition assistance: it
brings protocol settings, spatial planning, and image assessment into the
operator's existing workflow. Agents that use screenshots and standard input
actions can interact through this interface without requiring a dedicated
scanner-control API or direct access to internal acquisition state. This offers
a route to automation across heterogeneous console software while keeping
actions and visible outcomes available for operator review. It also creates a
demanding control problem: the agent must connect what is shown on screen to
acquisition decisions whose consequences appear in subsequent images.
Recent advances in general-purpose GUI agents make this interaction setting
increasingly relevant. Computer-use benchmarks evaluate multimodal agents on
stateful workflows over desktop applications and web services
\citep{yuan2026osworld2}. Medical acquisition poses a further question: can
such agents combine visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and
feedback-driven control to acquire the intended anatomy without human
correction during an episode? We ask not only whether an agent can operate the
machine, but whether its actions produce an acquisition that meets the intended
goal.
The distinction arises because acquisition actions determine what evidence
becomes available for subsequent decisions. We call this property
\emph{action-conditioned acquisition}: an agent action alters the acquisition
process and thereby changes the medical-image evidence produced at subsequent
steps. The agent must identify the anatomy on screen, relate image coordinates
to acquisition geometry, and use the resulting evidence to decide whether to
proceed or adjust. Changes to geometry, timing, or probe pose affect acquisition;
display-only adjustments do not. An agent can complete the prescribed workflow
and still acquire the wrong anatomy. Workflow completion alone does not
establish that the intended anatomy was acquired.
Existing environments address parts of this evaluation problem. Clinical
benchmarks cover electronic health records, simulated encounters, and
administrative workflows
\citep{jiang2025medagent,schmidgall2024agentclinic,bedi2026healthadmin}, while
MedCUA-Bench evaluates clinical GUI interaction with safety-critical errors
\citep{yu2026medcua}. These settings primarily concern records, software state,
or predefined observations rather than imaging acquisition. ABRA, RadABench,
and MedSPOT study post-acquisition viewing, radiology tool use, and interface
grounding \citep{maksudov2026abra,zheng2024radabench,shakeel2026medspot}; they
do not let the agent control the acquisition that generates the underlying
study. Autonomous MRI and MaRGE/MaRCoS address acquisition and scanner control
\citep{ravi2020autonomous,algarin2024marge}, but are MRI-specific systems rather
than standardized benchmarks for general-purpose GUI agents. The remaining
need is an evaluation setting that connects executable console workflows to
action-conditioned acquisition and independent anatomical ground truth.
To study this question, an environment must preserve the dependencies between
planning, acquisition, and assessment while retaining ground truth for the
acquired result. We introduce \textbf{MedImageOSWorld}, a benchmark with three
executable consoles: computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance (MR), and ultrasound. All three derive observations from
XCAT-based digital human anatomy phantoms \citep{segars2010xcat}. The environment couples
an order, a screening record, persistent patient and device state, a protocol
library, and an action-conditioned acquisition backend. Agents select and
configure protocols, plan anatomy-dependent slices, volumes, or views, acquire
images, and assess their adequacy. They can re-plan, re-acquire, repeat a view,
or escalate. Figure~\ref{fig:overview} separates the three stages that define
an episode: visible console interaction, a hidden physical-state transition,
and outcome evaluation against anatomical ground truth.
MedImageOSWorld provides a setting for studying how general-purpose agents
combine visual understanding, spatial reasoning, and feedback-driven control
in tasks with simulated physical consequences. A shared capability ladder
organizes these requirements and helps locate failure points. Evaluation
separates workflow completion from acquisition quality using hidden ground
truth in the digital subject's coordinate frame. This makes the target of
evaluation the connection between interface actions and measurable acquisition
outcomes, rather than procedural completion alone. Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Action-conditioned acquisition as an evaluation setting.} We
  formalize medical image acquisition as a GUI-agent task in which actions
  change the physical acquisition state and therefore the image evidence
  observed next. This setting separates two questions that existing
  benchmarks conflate: whether the agent completed the console workflow, and
  whether the resulting acquisition captured the intended anatomy.
  \item \textbf{MedImageOSWorld, a benchmark of executable scanner consoles.}
  Three simulated consoles (CT, MR, ultrasound) expose protocol selection,
  geometric planning, acquisition, review, and corrective actions through
  rendered screenshots and a constrained mouse-and-keyboard interface, with no
  access to interface or simulator state. 
  \item \textbf{Ground-truth scoring in the subject's coordinate frame.} Each
  committed acquisition is linked to the digital subject's coordinate frame,
  so a hidden oracle can grade geometry and
  anatomical coverage in millimetres, degrees, and coverage fractions
  without human assessment. Success, workflow progress, and acquisition quality
  are reported as three separate 0--100 scores, with environment faults kept
  apart as \texttt{INVALID}.
  \item \textbf{An empirical study of current GUI agents.} We evaluate
  11 open-weight models and two API-served proprietary models on 31,197 valid
  episodes included in scoring (30,513 for open-weight agents and 684 for
  proprietary agents) under a frozen interaction and scoring protocol. The best
  open-weight agent, Qwen3.8-27B, reaches a success rate of 25.0 but a
  workflow-progress rate of 74.5; no open-weight agent exceeds 12\
  millimetre-level planning, and CT remains nearly unsolved, with success at or
  below 1.5 for every open-weight agent. The simulator and data will be  available on
\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/neutral-123/MedImageOSWorld}{Hugging Face.}
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}
\textbf{General computer-use benchmarks.}
Table~\ref{tab:environment-comparison} contrasts representative clinical,
radiology, and acquisition environments across the interaction, acquisition,
and evaluation properties that define this task setting. OSWorld evaluates
multimodal agents by executed outcomes in real computer environments, and
OSWorld 2.0 extends this line to longer-horizon tasks
\citep{xie2024osworld,yuan2026osworld2}. AndroidWorld varies task parameters in
a dynamic mobile environment, while WebArena evaluates functional correctness
on realistic web tasks \citep{rawles2024androidworld,zhou2023webarena}. Like
these benchmarks, we score executed outcomes rather than action traces and use
task-specific parameter variation; MedImageOSWorld additionally introduces a
physical acquisition state that determines the next observation.
\textbf{Clinical and radiology agents.}
MedAgentBench and AgentClinic study EHR use and simulated encounters
\citep{jiang2025medagent,schmidgall2024agentclinic}; the health administration
benchmark and MedCUA-Bench cover administration and clinical GUI interaction
\citep{bedi2026healthadmin,yu2026medcua}. RadABench, MedSPOT, and ABRA study radiology
tool use, interface grounding, and DICOM viewing
\citep{zheng2024radabench,shakeel2026medspot,maksudov2026abra}. In these
settings, the relevant records or imaging study are fixed before the episode;
the agent does not control how the evidence is acquired. MedImageOSWorld adds
this acquisition loop before review or interpretation.
\textbf{Autonomous acquisition and digital subjects.}
Autonomous MRI supports automated MRI protocolling, planning, acquisition, and
reconstruction, while MaRGE/MaRCoS supports research MRI control
\citep{ravi2020autonomous,algarin2024marge}. These are MRI-specific acquisition
systems rather than benchmarks for general-purpose GUI agents. MedImageOSWorld
links console actions and committed acquisitions to the subject's coordinate
frame so that geometry and anatomical coverage can be scored automatically.
\FloatBarrier
\section{The MedImageOSWorld Environment}
\label{sec:method}
We model each episode as a partially observed interaction between an agent and a simulated console. The console state has two components. The \emph{physical acquisition state} determines what the scanner would acquire, such as the CT slab and isocentre, the MR imaging plane, or the ultrasound probe pose and tissue contact. The \emph{interface and workflow state} records the worklist, sequence queue, workflow stage, and display settings. At each step, the agent issues a single GUI action; the simulator then updates the console state using task-relevant physical abstractions. Display-only actions, such as adjusting window width and level, modify the interface state but leave the physical acquisition state unchanged. Section~\ref{sec:ground-truth} describes the separate evaluation of workflow completion and acquisition quality. Figure~\ref{fig:overview} illustrates this loop.

\subsection{Observation, action, and time}
The primary \textit{observation} is a PNG screenshot of the console rendered at a fixed viewport. The \textit{action} space consists of constrained mouse events and an allowlisted set of keyboard events, so the agent interacts through the same visible console and standard input modalities available to a human operator. The agent receives no DOM, accessibility tree, simulator or interface state, script-execution primitive, hidden UI-quality text, or direct scanner-control API; task geometry and the consequences of each action are therefore available only through the rendered pixels.
Before execution, a declared, version-fixed, deterministic codec may normalize model output into a legal action. For every step, an action receipt records the raw model output, any normalization or repair applied, whether the action was executed or rejected, and any additional feedback returned to the agent. Rejected actions consume steps as specified by the frozen interaction profile, and any model-specific repair logic or additional prompting is disclosed as part of the agent configuration. Simulated \textit{time} advances only through executed actions, including explicit wait actions, rather than during model inference.
\subsection{Three consoles}
All three consoles share a common structure (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}b):
planning controls modify the physical acquisition state, acquisition commits
it, and the acquired images provide evidence for assessment and correction.
\textbf{Computed tomography (CT).} After worklist and protocol selection, the agent plans on a scout image by
setting the scan slab, isocentre, monitoring region of interest (ROI), and
acquisition timing. The acquired stack is presented separately from the
prescription, so undercoverage can be detected and corrected. Task families
cover thoracic, renal, hepatic, and cardiac acquisition, including contrast
timing, repeat acquisition of clipped anatomy, and coverage under a dose-index
constraint.
\textbf{Magnetic resonance (MR).}
The agent prescribes imaging planes and volumes on localizer images by setting
plane position, orientation, field of view, and slab or slice coverage; each
acquisition reslices the digital subject at the committed geometry. Within the
sequence queue, acquired images guide the refinement or repetition of
subsequent prescriptions for cardiac cine planes, cardiac T1/T2 mapping, and
bilateral renal coverage.
\textbf{Ultrasound (US).}
The live renal image is rendered from the current probe position, orientation,
and tissue contact, and from the depth, frequency, and focus settings. Tasks
require searching for a kidney view, adjusting acquisition parameters,
distinguishing contact loss from inadequate gain, and freezing and saving a
selected frame.
\subsection{Digital subjects and ground truth}
\label{sec:ground-truth}
Benchmark episodes use virtual subjects in simulated consoles and involve no
scanning of humans or animals.
The digital anatomy phantoms provide registered anatomical structures in a
shared subject coordinate frame, in which every planning control and committed
acquisition is expressed. CT slabs and isocentres, MR planes and volumes, and
ultrasound probe planes can therefore be compared directly with hidden
anatomical masks and landmarks, enabling automatic measurement of endpoint and
centre error, plane position and orientation, field of view, and anatomical
coverage, independent of screen coordinates or click sequences.
Workflow checks use the interface state and event log to verify that required
stages and actions occurred, whereas the hidden oracle evaluates the anatomy
actually acquired; a workflow can thus complete without meeting the
acquisition-quality criteria. Rendering assumptions, coordinate conventions,
and modality-specific scope are documented in the supplementary section \textit{Simulator Rendering and Physical-Model Scope}.
\FloatBarrier
\section{Tasks and Capability Ladder}
\label{sec:ladder}
\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figure3_task_construction.png}
  \caption{\textbf{From acquisition procedures to executable benchmark tasks.}
  (a) The shared L0--L6 capability ladder is defined first; three medical
  imaging experts, assisted by a frontier AI model, propose, cross-review, and
  finalize each task. Each task specifies an initial state, an acquisition
  goal, an interaction budget, and scoring conditions. (b) A CT lung-coverage
  task links scout-based planning to the acquired volume, with workflow
  completion and anatomical coverage scored separately. Numbers in (b) are
  illustrative.}
  \label{fig:task-construction}
\end{figure*}
\paragraph{Task sourcing.}
We first defined the capability ladder and then designed tasks against it
(Figure~\ref{fig:task-construction}a). Three medical imaging experts, assisted
by a frontier AI model, proposed, cross-reviewed, and finalized each task.
The benchmark contains 49 task definitions: 8 for CT, 34 for MR, and 7 for
ultrasound. They cover CT coverage planning,
dose constraints, and undercoverage recovery; MR console operation, acquisition
planning, mapping, and coverage assessment; and ultrasound kidney operation,
measurement, search, optimization, and fault recovery. The tasks evaluate
acquisition operations, not diagnostic accuracy.
The supplementary section ``Task Catalog and Reproducibility Details'' lists
every task with a short description and its capability level; execution coverage
is reported separately from task membership.
\paragraph{Capability ladder.}
A task's level is the capability it targets, not the interaction mechanism it
uses (Figure~\ref{fig:task-construction}a). L0--L1 concern operating the console,
L2 concerns interpreting the current observation, and L3--L6 add spatial
quantification, physical constraints, temporal closure, and recovery. A
composite task is counted once, at its primary level; for example,
\path{ct_ui_smoke_routine} completes the full routine workflow but is placed at
L3 because it is gated on lung geometry. The ladder helps locate where
performance breaks down, but it is not a psychometrically validated scale, and
a single failure does not identify a unique cause: a planning failure may
originate in an earlier perception error.
\paragraph{Task specification.} Each task is defined by its goal text, modality, capability level, reset
distribution, observation and action profile, step and wall-time budgets,
termination conditions, ground-truth scorer, and task and scorer versions. A
task may define multiple conditions, and each condition targets 30 digital
human subjects with three seeds per subject. Proprietary agents are evaluated
on the first five assets of each task in the frozen order. The episode
manifest distinguishes task definitions, conditions, planned slots, attempts,
and scored episodes, and records the subject, seed, bundle, and reset
information associated with each.
\section{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:scoring}
\paragraph{Verdicts.}
The task scorer assigns \texttt{PASS}, \texttt{PARTIAL}, \texttt{FAIL}, or an
undetermined outcome. Environment, receipt, or scorer faults are
\texttt{INVALID}. Slots left unrun after a confirmed model-side early stop are
counted as failures in SR. \texttt{INVALID} episodes and slots lost to
infrastructure faults are excluded from metric denominators and reported
separately.
\paragraph{Workflow and acquisition are scored separately.}
Workflow checks cover required and forbidden events and the terminal state.
Acquisition quality is measured against hidden ground truth in the digital
subject's frame: geometry in millimetres and degrees, and coverage as the
fraction of the target structure inside the acquired volume. Coverage is
computed from the acquired slab, never inferred from the prescribed range or a
completion button (Figure~\ref{fig:task-construction}b). Thresholds are task-
and scorer-version specific; for the MR \texttt{L4\_2ch} task, the current
relaxed engineering profile gates centre, normal, field of view, and landmark
errors at 8~mm, 5~degrees, 10~mm, and 5~mm. Continuous components remain
visible alongside every verdict.
\paragraph{Protocol freeze and aggregation.}
A valid comparison freezes the task version, subject or bundle, reset,
observation and action profile, budgets, scorer and thresholds, runtime, and
agent configuration. Task-side manifests are shared across compared agents;
agent-side prompts, codecs, deterministic normalizations, repair policies, and
extra feedback may differ and are disclosed. Step accounting follows the
frozen profile for rejected outputs, repairs, and corrective feedback;
transport-level retries are logged separately. Results are laid out as model
$\times$ modality $\times$ level
$\times$ observation condition, with empty modality--level cells shown as N/A.
We report three 0--100 metrics. Success rate (SR) is the percentage of
registered slots that satisfy the task's complete success criterion. Progress
rate (PR) is the mean percentage of registered workflow progress completed per
slot. Acquisition quality (AQ) is the mean registered, normalized quality of
the acquired result, computed from task-specific hidden-ground-truth measures.
The legacy \texttt{PARTIAL} verdict provides no fractional credit to any main
metric. Task-specific geometry, coverage, gate values, exhausted-budget rates,
and the counts and reasons for \texttt{INVALID} episodes are reported alongside
SR, PR, and AQ.
Conditions are weighted equally within each task; the clean and defect
conditions of MR renal adequacy each contribute half of its task score.
Condition-specific results include answer frequencies, no-answer rates, and
actual denominators after the exclusions defined above. Intervals resample
subjects with their repeated runs grouped.
The official scorer identity is the tuple of scorer code digest, oracle digest,
and threshold version; changing any element creates a new scorer version.
\paragraph{Overall score.}
Let $s_{ij}$ be a model's SR proportion for task $j$ at level $i$, after
condition aggregation and frozen denominator rules. The L0--L6 aggregate uses
$w_i=i+1$:
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{Score}=100\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{6}(i+1)\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}s_{ij}}
 {\sum_{i=0}^{6}(i+1)n_i},\qquad 0\leq s_{ij}\leq1.
  \label{eq:overall-score}
\end{equation}
Here $n_i$ counts task definitions; the current denominator is 181. Higher
levels receive greater pre-selected weight, not empirically validated
psychometric difficulty. Modality and level scores are also reported. The
pooled SR score is not modality-equal. SR, PR, and AQ are reported side by side
and never merged.
\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}
\subsection{Setup}
We ask four questions. Which registered requirements can current GUI agents
satisfy across modalities and capability levels? How often does workflow
completion coincide with acquisition quality? At which observation or
corrective gate do non-passing episodes stop making progress? How sensitive are
scores to the agent harness when the task-side protocol is held fixed?
We evaluate eleven open-weight GUI and vision-language agents:
Qwen3.8-27B, UI-Mate-27B, GUI-Owl-1.5-32B-Instruct,
GUI-Owl-1.5-32B-Thinking, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct,
Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking, UI-TARS-1.5-7B,
Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Instruct, OpenCUA-32B, Gemma-4-31B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B.
All are served locally with greedy decoding (temperature 0). We additionally
evaluate OpenAI GPT-6 Sol (\texttt{gpt-6-sol}) and Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5
(\texttt{claude-opus-5-5}) through their provider APIs. 
The target design assigns each task condition 30 subjects $\times$ 3 seeds.
With clean and defect conditions, MR renal adequacy therefore has 180 planned
slots per model. The frozen manifest records actual attempts, outcomes,
exclusions, and unrun slots, together with the agent configuration for each
condition.
Hardware allocation and proprietary-agent harness versions are summarized in
the supplementary material. Full prompts, action-codec specifications, and
run configurations will be released through our
\href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/neutral-123/MedImageOSWorld}{Hugging Face repository}.
\subsection{Main results}
Figure~\ref{fig:capability-heatmap} summarizes performance across tasks and

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
MedImageOSWorld provides a controlled setting for studying how general-purpose
multimodal agents apply their capabilities to specialized acquisition tasks.
The interaction primitives remain screenshots, clicks, drags, and keyboard
input, while successful actions depend on anatomy, acquisition geometry, and
the current subject. An agent must combine interface operation with domain
knowledge and visual reasoning to turn an acquisition goal into a working
prescription. The gap between workflow progress and task success makes this
combination a useful target for evaluating the transfer of general-purpose
agents to specialized visual workflows.
The results show where this combination currently breaks down. Success drops
sharply at geometric planning, where agents must translate two-dimensional
views into a position, orientation, and extent in the subject's coordinate
frame. Their acquisition choices then determine the images available for the
next decision. In renal and CT recovery tasks, agents frequently reach the
review stage without making an effective adjustment; some also alter an
adequate acquisition in clean cases. Together, these findings point to
difficulties in connecting visual evidence to the choice and verification of
a corrective action. The logs do not isolate whether a failure begins with
anatomical interpretation, coordinate mapping, control selection, or
execution. Continuous geometry and coverage measurements help locate the
resulting error, while task-specific gates record whether the required
recovery procedure was followed.
This setting also allows future evaluations to ask whether general model
upgrades improve acquisition outcomes without additional domain
demonstrations, and how much a small number of expert demonstrations can
help. Comparing these conditions on held-out subjects and task variations
would test how readily agents adapt their existing capabilities to acquisition
workflows. Improvements should be assessed through acquisition quality and
task success alongside workflow progress, especially on planning and recovery
tasks. Continuous outcome measures can detect useful changes before an
acquisition crosses a binary success threshold. Such comparisons need fixed
task and scorer versions, subjects, reset conditions, and budgets, with model
revisions and harness changes recorded separately.
Interpreting these comparisons requires accounting for both training exposure
and evaluation conditions. The evaluated models' prior exposure to related
interfaces or procedures is not established, so the present results do not
isolate generalization to unseen training domains. Proprietary agents also
use fewer subjects and provider-specific harnesses, which limits attribution
of their advantage to the underlying models. The simulated consoles measure
selected anatomical and parameter objectives; transfer to scanner hardware,
diagnostic image quality, and the benefit of human oversight require further
evaluation. Within these limits, the benchmark makes it possible to examine
whether gains in general-purpose agents translate into more effective
acquisition decisions.
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
MedImageOSWorld evaluates general-purpose GUI agents on 49 medical acquisition
tasks across simulated CT, MR, and ultrasound consoles. Current agents often
advance through the workflow while failing to achieve the required geometry
or make effective corrections. By linking interface actions to acquired images
and hidden anatomical ground truth, the benchmark measures how visual
understanding is translated into acquisition outcomes. It provides a
controlled setting for studying whether improvements in multimodal agents
carry over to specialized tasks that require spatial planning and
feedback-driven action.

paper.title: Can Multimodal Decision Models Classify Breast Ultrasound Images? Benchmarking CLEF and CLEF-Flash Across Prompts and Datasets
paper.abstract: Multimodal decision models return probabilities over predefined alternatives, offering a structured interface for image classification. This study benchmarks inference with CLEF and CLEF-Flash on 2818 breast ultrasound images from Dataset B, BUSI, and BUS-BRA. Dataset B and BUS-BRA use binary benign-malignant classification, whereas BUSI includes normal, benign, and malignant categories. Model parameters remain unchanged, and original images are submitted without user-defined preprocessing. Three prompts provide minimal labels, an explicit classification task, or sonographic criteria. We report accuracy, macro F1, balanced accuracy, macro precision, throughput, and latency. CLEF-Flash with the clinical prompt achieves the highest accuracy on all three datasets: 74.85% on Dataset B, 66.28% on BUSI, and 51.63% on BUS-BRA. On BUSI, however, CLEF with the task-guided prompt achieves the highest macro F1 (64.51%) and balanced accuracy (68.72%). CLEF-Flash has lower latency in every matched comparison. Clinical instructions improve CLEF-Flash accuracy relative to the minimal prompt but reduce CLEF accuracy on all datasets. Confusion matrices reveal frequent benign-to-malignant errors, particularly on BUS-BRA, where all configurations fall below the 67.63% accuracy of a majority-class predictor. These findings demonstrate dataset-and prompt-dependent performance and motivate class-specific evaluation before applying multimodal decision models to breast ultrasound analysis.

paper.title: Radiomics-Based Thyroid Nodule Classification with Label-Conditional Conformal Prediction
paper.abstract: Thyroid nodule malignancy assessment relies on ultrasound imaging, yet current risk stratification systems suffer from substantial interobserver variability, contributing to a high rate of unnecessary biopsies. We propose a radiomics-based framework combining quantitative feature extraction via PyRadiomics with a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) classifier, selected among six candidates for its favorable trade-off between discriminative performance and interpretability. To complement point predictions with uncertainty estimates, Cross-Conformal Prediction with label-conditional guarantees is applied, flagging ambiguous cases for clinical review rather than forcing a binary decision. Experiments are conducted on TN5000, a publicly available ultrasound dataset of thyroid nodules. After Spearman correlation filtering, 36 features are retained and the GAM achieves an AUC of $0.89$, a sensitivity of $0.83$, and a specificity of $0.82$ on the validation set. At a significance level $ε=0.09$, selected to ensure empirical coverage guarantees on both classes, 63\% of nodules on the test set receive a certain (i.e., single-label) prediction, with conditional precision of $0.94$ for certain malignant and conditional Negative Predictive Value (NPV) of $0.73$ for certain benign cases, while the remaining 37\% are referred to the clinician.

paper.title: How well do routinely collected demographic and clinical variables aid point-of-care lung ultrasound TB classification
paper.abstract: We consider the fusion of lung ultrasound images with routinely-collected clinical and demographic data for the purpose of automated tuberculosis (TB) screening using deep-learning. Such deep-learning based screening tools for TB could meaningfully support the health care system in Africa, where the burden of disease is severe and resources are constrained. Beginning with an established ResNet baseline for classification of lung ultrasound images, which achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) curve of 0.91 [0.86,0.96] (95% CI), we consider the incorporation of the clinical and demographic data using three fusion approaches. We find that a simple average-based fusion of the output scores of separately-trained image and clinical data classifiers consistently matches or outperforms a more complex approach where the data is fused earlier and a combined classifier is trained. Fusing the image and the clinical classifiers in this way leads to a classifier with an overall AUROC of 0.95 [0.91,0.99] (specificity of 0.76 at sensitivity 0.93) which is an improvement of 4% absolute over the image-only baseline. We also find that greedy feature selection can be used to reduce the number of clinical and demographic inputs without sacrificing classification performance. Finally, when we differentiate between clinical and demographic data that are self-reported, that require some basic measurement or calculation, and that require a point-of-care (POC) test, we find the inclusion of the POC tests included in this study to be of minimal benefit to classification performance. We conclude that the incorporation of routinely-collected clinical and demographic data is a promising way to improve the performance of lung ultrasound based automatic classification.

paper.title: Variational Bayesian Inference Based Progressive Multi-Target MIMO Sensing with Nuisance Parameters
paper.abstract: This paper proposes a progressive Bayesian multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) sensing framework for multiple targets over multiple stages. We consider a practical yet challenging scenario where the targets' angles are unknown and random parameters to be estimated, while the targets' reflection coefficients are unknown nuisance parameters. With an initial prior probability density function (PDF) for the targets' angles, we progressively update the prior PDF for each sensing stage as the posterior PDF obtained from the previous stage, based on which Bayesian transmit beamforming optimization is performed to minimize the sum posterior Cramér-Rao bound (PCRB) in estimating the targets' angles and Bayesian sensing is performed with the help of new observations in this stage. To analytically characterize the intractable and high-dimensional posterior PDF with low complexity, we propose a variational Bayesian inference based approach which derives a surrogate posterior PDF in closed form with only polynomial complexity over the number of targets, in sharp contrast to existing numerical calculation approaches with exponential complexity. Numerical results validate the efficacy of our proposed framework in progressively refining sensing performance.

paper.title: On the Performance of Randomly Generated Codebooks in Near-Field Communications
paper.abstract: Near-field communication with large antenna arrays requires beamforming techniques that account for spherical wavefront effects. While predefined codebooks are widely used in multiple-antenna wireless systems, the performance of randomly generated codebooks in the near-field region has not been investigated. In this work, we study four randomly generated codebooks for near-field communications: random vector quantization (RVQ), random phase (RP), random far-field (RFF), and random near-field (RNF) codebooks. We use the known RVQ gain distribution as a benchmark. For RP, we derive a large-array bulk approximation and characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RNF, we characterize the high-gain tail behavior of the gain distribution. For RFF, we derive an analytical approximation for the maximum achievable beamforming gain when far-field beams are used to serve near-field users, along with the corresponding maximizing far-field direction. We also analyze the maximum-gain scaling with codebook size. Monte Carlo simulations verify the analytical results and show that RVQ and RP degrade significantly as the array size increases, while RNF achieves the most favorable high-gain scaling. RFF can outperform RVQ and RP for finite codebook sizes, but its maximum gain saturates below one due to the phase mismatch between the far-field beams and the near-field channel. These results show how codebook structure, array size, and codebook size affect random beamforming performance in the near-field.

paper.title: Conformal Risk Control for Multiuser Beamforming
paper.abstract: We consider multiuser downlink beamforming with prescribed signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirements under imperfect channel state information and a tight transmit power budget. Robust worst-case designs often require tractable channel-error models and may not yield feasible beamformers that meet the power budget. To alleviate these issues, we propose conformal risk control for beamforming (CRCBeam), which combines the classical fixed-point minimum-power beamforming with conformal risk control to calibrate an SINR margin from calibration sample pairs of estimated and true channels. Under exchangeability, CRCBeam provides finite-sample control over served-outage risk, which is the probability of transmitting when at least one user fails to meet its SINR target. CRCBeam requires no parametric channel-error model and transmits only when the power budget is met. Numerical experiments using a pilot contamination channel error model corroborate that CRCBeam achieves the served-outage risk while meeting the power budget. In contrast, worst-case robust baselines, Gaussian-ball and conformal-ball beamforming, either do not meet the target risk or exceed the power budget.

paper.title: ARISE: Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation for Interpretable IBD Assessment
paper.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) requires frequent imaging-based assessment, yet interpretation of modalities such as wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) and intestinal ultrasound remains heavily dependent on specialist expertise. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) demonstrate significant potential in multimodal medical image analysis, but their clinical adoption is hindered by their insufficient domain-specific reasoning, susceptibility to hallucination, scarcity of high quality training data in fine-grained diagnostics and limited interpretability. We introduce ARISE (Adaptive Agentic Reasoning with Image-grounded Self-Evaluation), an autonomous planning framework that models few-shot medical image understanding as a sequential agentic workflow. ARISE structures agent execution into a transparent 5-stage workflow: hypothesis generation, image-grounded evidence summarization, evidence-conditioned refinement, symbolic verification, and final diagnosis. We apply ARISE to IBD assessment across two independent patient cohorts: wireless capsule endoscopy (WCE) images for Crohn's disease and B-mode ultrasound data for ulcerative colitis. ARISE consistently improves diagnostic performance over baseline VLMs while exposing where reasoning succeeds or fails, providing a more interpretable basis for clinical decision support and realistic deployment.

paper.title: EchoDino: A pediatric foundation model for transferable echocardiographic analysis across the lifespan
paper.abstract: Echocardiography is the most widely used cardiac imaging modality, yet interpretation demands integrating visual evidence across global anatomy, localized structures and dynamic cardiac motion. Machine-learning models have automated individual tasks, but they are typically built for a single purpose and depend on expensively labeled datasets - a barrier particularly acute in pediatric care, where data are scarce and anatomy changes with age. Here we present EchoDino, a self-supervised foundation model for echocardiography, created by adapting the DINOv3 framework to 3.7 million frames from 1.7 million unlabeled pediatric echocardiography videos. With its encoder frozen, EchoDino produces representations that capture global context, local anatomy, and dense spatial detail. We introduce Motion-biased Entropy Maximization Sampling (MEMS) to select the most informative frames for video-level analysis. Across nine pediatric and adult datasets, EchoDino outperformed strong baseline models, raising view-classification accuracy from 0.609 to 0.889 and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for structural-heart-disease detection from 0.811 to 0.872, while also cutting age-estimation error from 3.857 to 1.389 years, achieving the best segmentation accuracy and lowering ejection-fraction errors. By generalizing from label-free pediatric data to adult echocardiography, EchoDino offers a versatile foundation for cardiac image analysis across the lifespan.

paper.title: Decouple, Purify and Unite: Semantic-Structural Prototype Learning for Federated Medical Segmentation
paper.abstract: Federated learning enables medical institutions to train a global model without sharing data, yet feature heterogeneity from diverse scanners or protocols remains challenging. Existing representation-based methods face two limitations: 1) Incomplete Contextual Representation Learning: single-layer or coupled representations overlook multi-level structural cues and entangle regional semantics with boundary details. 2) Layerwise Style and Aggregation Biases: domain-specific style discrepancies across intermediate layers degrade prototypes, while aggregation that overlooks client distribution shifts can further amplify bias. We propose FedBCS+, federated decoupled contextual alignment with style-purified aggregation. We employ Frequency-domain Style Recalibration (FSR) in prototype construction to decouple content-style representations and extract style-purified prototypes. Built upon these purified features, Decoupled Contextual Prototype Alignment (DCPA) explicitly decouples multi-level features into semantic and structural prototypes and aligns regional semantics and fine-grained anatomical structures separately. Style-purified Semantic Prototype Aggregation (S2PA) measures each client's purified prototype divergence from the global consensus and adaptively reweights aggregation toward under-represented clients to reduce consensus bias. On five heterogeneous medical segmentation benchmarks spanning histopathology, MRI, ultrasound, and colonoscopy, FedBCS+ achieves the highest mean Dice among the compared methods. A convergence analysis further characterizes how aggregation and alignment affect the optimization bound.

paper.title: Beyond Explanation: Debugging Medical Imaging Models via Concept Intervention
paper.abstract: Medical imaging models often operate as black boxes, limiting interpretability and systematic debugging. We introduce an easy-to-use, plug-and-play framework for concept-based interpretation and model refinement. By aligning a single-modality encoder to BioMedCLIP, we construct a Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM) that enables concept-level interventions. These interventions allow us to isolate causal versus spuriously correlated concepts, validate insights with domain experts, and generate counterfactual samples for targeted fine-tuning. We evaluate our framework on a Mayo Clinic ultrasound dataset and the CheXpert 5x200 chest X-ray dataset. Results demonstrate that concept intervention enables reliable model diagnosis while maintaining, and occasionally improving predictive performance via guided fine-tuning. Our findings highlight the practical value of this framework for controlled, interpretable refinement of clinical deep learning models.
